practices.practice: Create a single shared MongoClient / Mongoose connection per process (singleton) and reuse it rather than opening many short-lived clients.
practices.prior_belief: Use a single shared Mongoose connection per process (reuse the mongoose connection across modules) rather than creating many short-lived connections; size the pool instead of spinning up more processes to avoid connection storms.

practices.practice: Tune driver connection options to your environment (pool sizing, timeouts and maxIdleTimeMS) and pick different sensible defaults for serverless vs long-running processes.
practices.prior_belief: Tune Mongo/Mongoose connection options: set maxPoolSize to a value appropriate for the VM (e.g., 50–200 per process), serverSelectionTimeoutMS (e.g., 30000), and socketTimeoutMS (e.g., 120000) to avoid long blocking when the cluster is transiently unreachable.
practices.how_found: documentdb-connection

practices.practice: Enable driver retryable reads/writes where supported and implement application-level exponential backoff + jitter (and respect Retry-After / retry-after-ms headers) for throttling and transient faults.
practices.prior_belief: Handle transient rate-limiting (HTTP 429 / Mongo mapped throttling) by reading the server Retry-After/Retry-After-ms where available, implementing exponential backoff with jitter, and consider reducing batch size or increasing RU/s when 429s are frequent.
practices.how_found: Azure DocumentDB throttling Retry-After 429 guidance

practices.practice: For large scans use server-side cursors/getMore with a controlled batchSize (cursor + batchSize) instead of fetching all documents at once.
practices.prior_belief: When scanning all active accounts, use a server cursor with pagination (find().batchSize(500) / cursor.each or async iteration) and projection to return only fields needed for interest calculation (e.g., _id, balance, rate, status) to limit memory and RU consumption.
practices.how_found: Azure DocumentDB cursor batchSize getMore

practices.practice: Avoid skip/offset pagination for large scans because it becomes inefficient and unstable; prefer range-based or cursor-based pagination (e.g., sort by a unique key and use > lastSeenId).
practices.prior_belief: Avoid skip-based pagination for large scans; use range-based pagination (e.g., sort by _id or lastModified and use > lastSeenId) or an explicit cursor so each batch is efficient and repeatable.
practices.how_found: avoid skip-based pagination Azure DocumentDB skip performance

practices.practice: Apply projection (return only fields needed) and, in Mongoose, prefer lean() when you don't need full Mongoose documents to reduce memory and driver overhead.
practices.prior_belief: When reading accounts for computation, use projection and lean() (Mongoose) to avoid full Mongoose document overhead; e.g., Account.find(query).select('balance rate _id').lean().cursor().batchSize(500).
practices.how_found: documentdb-query-optimizer

practices.practice: Create a partial (filtered) index that only indexes active interest-bearing accounts to reduce index size and RU cost for large scans.
practices.prior_belief: Create an index tuned for the scanning query on accounts: a partial or filtered index that only indexes active interest-bearing accounts (e.g., partialFilterExpression: { status: 'active', interestEnabled: true } and include fields used in projection) to reduce RU and I/O.

practices.practice: Create a unique compound index on the journal (for example accountId + runDate) to enforce idempotency so duplicate inserts for the same day fail with duplicate-key errors you can detect and ignore.
practices.prior_belief: Enforce idempotency by creating a unique compound index on the journal collection (e.g., { accountId: 1, accrualDate: 1 }) so repeated accrual runs produce duplicate-key errors you can detect and ignore.

practices.practice: Create indexes idempotently at deployment/migration time and verify index existence before running large scans to avoid runtime index builds during high-load jobs.
practices.prior_belief: Create indexes at deployment/migration time idempotently (createIndex with background where supported), and verify index existence before producing large scans; do not rely on implicit index creation at runtime during high-load jobs.

practices.practice: Monitor request charge (RUs), RU/s utilization and 429 counts (throttling), enable diagnostic/slow-query logging, and alert on saturation so you can scale or reduce batch sizes before jobs fail.
practices.prior_belief: Monitor RU/s, RU consumption per operation, request charge on queries, and 429 counts in metrics and set alerts (e.g., when RU% > 70% or 429s increase) so you can scale RU or reduce batch sizes before jobs start failing.

practices.practice: Use unordered bulk writes (ordered: false) to maximize throughput and tune batch size and concurrency for your cluster; avoid extremely large single requests that exceed service limits.
practices.prior_belief: Write journal entries with unordered bulkWrite({ ordered: false }) in moderate batches (commonly 200–1000 ops per batch) to maximize throughput while avoiding huge single requests that spike RU and risk partial failures.

practices.practice: Treat bulkWrite partial failures as an expected outcome: inspect results and writeErrors, retry only idempotent operations, and suppress/handle duplicate-key (11000) errors when using unique constraints for idempotency.
practices.prior_belief: Treat bulkWrite partial failures as normal: inspect bulkWriteResult and writeErrors, retry only idempotent operations (or those that failed due to transient errors) and suppress duplicate-key errors (11000) when enforcing idempotency via unique index.

practices.practice: Store date/time values in UTC using ISO 8601 format so queries and range filters behave predictably across time zones.
practices.prior_belief: Store accrual timestamps in UTC (ISO 8601) and use a single canonical accrualDate key used by the unique index so different processes/runs compute the same journal key and idempotency works across time zones.

practices.practice: Use TTL indexes (expireAfterSeconds) on collections when you need automatic eviction/retention instead of frequent updates or deletions of many documents.
practices.prior_belief: Keep journal documents immutable (never update an accrual document) and, if retention is required, use a TTL index (expireAfterSeconds) on the journal collection rather than updating/removing documents frequently.

practices.practice: Keep documents reasonably small (well under the 16 MB BSON limit) and avoid very wide documents so reads/writes and indexes consume fewer RUs.
practices.prior_belief: Limit document size and the amount of indexed data per document (avoid wide documents) so reads/writes consume fewer RUs and indexes remain small; keep accrual journal entries compact (only accountId, accrualDate, amount, metadata).

practices.practice: Do not depend on multi-document transactions for high-throughput journal/archival workflows; transactions are supported only with limitations (unsharded collections, timeouts), so prefer idempotent single-document writes or test transaction support thoroughly before production use.
practices.prior_belief: Do not rely on multi-document transactions for high-throughput archival/journal workloads; prefer idempotent single-document writes and unique constraints. If transactions are required, test support on the target server version before using them in production.

practices.practice: When using vector-capable clusters, configure vector index parameters (DiskANN / HNSW / IVF) at index creation time and tune per-query search parameters (efSearch / lSearch) rather than reconstructing indexes in hot paths.
practices.prior_belief: When working with vector-capable clusters, keep vector index parameter tuning out of hot paths: configure HNSW / DiskANN parameters (M, efConstruction, index type) at index creation time and set ef (efSearch) per query to trade recall/latency; avoid creating vector indexes with overly large construction params during daily jobs.

notes:
I first inspected the sample app to see which areas matter (connection handling, singleton client, cursor-based batching, partial and unique indexes, unordered bulk writes, UTC timestamps and immutability, monitoring, and vector-index-capable cluster). I searched Microsoft Learn and loaded several installed skills that contain focused guidance for Azure DocumentDB (connection, driver, indexing, query optimization, vector search, security, monitoring, data modeling, local deployment). Public Microsoft docs confirm most of the prior beliefs (connection via env/Key Vault, TLS required, Private Link, singleton client pattern, pool tuning, cursor/batchSize, avoid skip, partial/unique/TTL indexes, index creation guidance, monitoring RUs and 429 handling, using Retry-After and backoff, transaction limitations, document size limits, and CMK/Key Vault practices). A few prior beliefs are not present as explicit numeric rules in the public docs (for example a precise recommended unordered bulkWrite batch size like '200–1000 ops'); these are left as prior_knowledge_only in the searches_with_no_useful_result list so the product team can see where the public record is silent.
